h1: Brewery consultancy for a brewpub and for a large plant: what changes
title: Brewery Consultancy by Plant Size | Craft Beer School
desc: How brewery consultancy differs for a small brewpub and a large plant: what each owner needs, where the risks sit and how we work with both.
teaser: A 500-litre brewpub and a 100-hectolitre plant share a recipe and almost nothing else.
standfirst: The principles of brewing stay the same as a brewery grows. The problems do not. This guide sets out what changes with size and what stays constant, so you can ask a consultant the right questions.
sections:
Wort is still wort. Yeast needs oxygen at pitching, a healthy cell count and a temperature it likes. Sanitation matters at every scale. A diacetyl rest is still a diacetyl rest.

A good consultant brings that knowledge to both ends of the market. What differs is where the money leaks and which decisions are hard to undo.
The brewpub: small volume, many roles

A brewpub usually has one brewer, sometimes two. That person brews, cleans, packs, orders and often tastes for quality alone. The risks are people risks first.

Typical consultancy work for a brewpub covers the following.

  • Choosing a brewhouse size that matches realistic sales, since the vessels are the hardest thing to change later
  • Laying out the room so cleaning, grain handling and cold storage work in a small footprint
  • Writing simple recipes and process sheets that a new brewer can follow
  • Setting up a basic quality routine: gravity, pH, temperature and a tasting log
  • Planning the mix of draught, packaged and seasonal beers

Quality in a brewpub often depends on one person. A written process is the insurance.
The large plant: systems, not people

A large plant has a team and a shift pattern. Problems come from losses that nobody sees because each department looks only at its own number.

Consultancy here leans on measurement. Brewhouse efficiency, cold side losses, packaging line efficiency, water and energy per hectolitre and yield from malt to saleable beer all need to be tracked and compared month to month. A small percentage gain in a large plant is real money.

Large plants also need documented quality systems, trained supervisors, preventive maintenance and planned changeovers between products. A consultant helps design these and checks that the team can run them without outside help.

Many breweries sit between the two. They outgrow a brewpub model but have not yet built the systems of a large plant. This is where growth hurts: the founder still wants to taste every batch while volume has doubled.

If you are planning to expand, start with the numbers. A project report for a brewery expansion tests whether demand, equipment and cash line up before you order a new tank.

Rahul Baliyan leads on brewing: process, recipes, brewhouse practice and team supervision. Ankur Napa leads on quality systems, costing and data. Which of them works on your project depends on what you need.

Most engagements start with a health check of the plant as it is, a written action plan and then support on the items you choose. We aim to leave your team able to run what we set up. Work is remote by video call and shared data, with site visits by arrangement.

We do not quote results in advance. Every plant starts from a different place. A promise of a fixed gain would be a guess.

Ask who will actually do the work. Ask what you will have in your hands at the end: a report, a procedure, a trained person. Ask how they handle excise and licensing. A good answer points you to a state licensing adviser. A poor one waves the topic away. Ask for a plan you can follow without them. Our guide on independent reviews of project reports shows the same scepticism applied to documents.
Where the money leaks at each scale

In a brewpub the leaks are small but constant: beer lost to a hose left running, a batch dumped after a missed cleaning step, kegs that do not come back. Nobody sees the total because nobody adds it up.

In a large plant the leaks hide inside the process. Wort left in the lauter tun, beer lost to the yeast and filter at the cellar, fills that run over target and broken packaging all look minor. Added across a year of output they are not.

A consultant's first useful contribution at either scale is a loss account: where product goes between the mash tun and the customer, measured in litres. You cannot fix what you have not counted. Start with a simple monthly table and let the trend show you where to look next.
faqs: Is a consultant worth it for a small brewpub?
Often yes, at the planning stage, because the biggest decisions such as vessel sizes and layout are hardest to undo. After opening, a short health check can be enough.
Do you only work with breweries in India?
Our experience is built in India. The work runs remotely, so location is not a barrier. Rules for licensing and excise depend on where the plant sits. Check them locally.
Can you help a plant that is already running badly?
Yes. We start with a health check of yield, losses, quality and costs, then agree a written action plan. We do not promise a figure before we have seen your data.
